title: Sustainable high-performance concrete with crumb rubber and ternary supplementary cementitious materials via experimental microstructural and statistical analysis
abstract: Abstract In response to growing concerns regarding construction waste management and the depletion of natural resources, this study investigates sustainable concrete mixtures incorporating crumb rubber, shredded rubber, fly ash, silica fume, and marble slurry powder. Twenty concrete mixtures were prepared to examine the combined effects of rubber aggregates and supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs) on mechanical properties, durability performance, and microstructural characteristics. The results show that, although rubber incorporation reduced strength, the use of SCMs partially offset this effect. Compressive, split tensile, and flexural strengths increased by up to 12%, 8%, and 10%, respectively, compared with their respective rubber-modified reference mixes. Durability indicators, including chloride migration and water absorption, were reduced by approximately 15–20%, indicating improved resistance to fluid ingress. These improvements are attributed to the pozzolanic activity and filler effects of the mineral additions, which promoted pore refinement and improved matrix continuity. Microstructural observations revealed denser interfacial transition zones and more uniform hydration products, supporting the observed trends in mechanical and transport behaviour. Regression-based analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to evaluate the relative influence of the selected variables within the experimental domain, identifying crumb rubber content as the dominant factor affecting mechanical performance, with coefficients of determination ranging from 0.81 to 0.97. The findings demonstrate that carefully proportioned SCM systems combined with controlled rubber incorporation can produce durable and resource-efficient concrete suitable for non-structural and lightly loaded components where serviceability, durability, and waste utilisation are key design considerations.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The rapid global expansion of infrastructure, including transportation networks, residential developments, and commercial construction, has led to a substantial increase in the demand for raw materials while simultaneously intensifying the generation of construction and demolition waste. In the absence of sustainable material strategies, significant volumes of this waste are disposed of in landfills, while continued extraction and processing of virgin resources accelerate environmental degradation. To address these concurrent challenges, the concrete industry has increasingly adopted circular economy principles through the incorporation of industrial byproducts and waste-derived materials into cementitious systems. Such strategies aim to reduce carbon emissions, conserve natural resources, and improve material efficiency [ 1 ].

Concrete occupies a central position in this transition. As the most widely used construction material worldwide, its extensive application is driven by its adaptability, structural capacity, cost-effectiveness, and ease of placement. Conventional concrete is composed of cement, fine and coarse aggregates, water, and mineral or chemical admixtures, each contributing to its fresh and hardened properties [ 2 ]. Among these constituents, cement production is the most environmentally intensive process. On a global scale, cement manufacture accounts for approximately 7–8% of total CO₂ emissions, largely due to energy-intensive clinker production and associated fossil fuel consumption [ 3 ].

In response to these environmental concerns, considerable research has focused on the use of supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs), such as fly ash (FA), silica fume (SF), and marble slurry powder (MSP), as partial replacements for cement. These industrial byproducts are valued for their pozzolanic reactivity and their ability to enhance mechanical performance and durability when appropriately incorporated into concrete mixtures [ 4 ]. FA and SF are well established for improving long-term strength and reducing permeability, while MSP, owing to its fine particle size and calcium-rich composition, primarily acts as a microfiller that refines pore structure and enhances cohesiveness, particularly in mixtures requiring improved workability [ 5 ].

The marble and granite processing industries generate substantial quantities of waste during cutting, polishing, and finishing operations. In certain regions, it has been reported that up to 80% of quarried stone is lost in the form of slurry and fine particulate matter [ 6 ]. Recent investigations indicate that marble powder can be effectively utilised as a partial replacement for fine aggregates in non-structural and semi-structural concretes, where it contributes to improved cohesiveness and reduced environmental impact without adversely affecting workability [ 7 ]. Beyond sustainability benefits, waste-derived materials have also demonstrated enhancements in mechanical performance, thermal insulation behaviour, and long-term durability under a range of exposure conditions [ 8 ].

SCMs further contribute to durability enhancement by mitigating chloride ingress, sulphate attack, and alkali-silica reaction through matrix densification and secondary hydration processes [ 9 ]. However, efforts to improve ductility, toughness, and impact resistance have prompted investigations beyond mineral byproducts alone. Crumb rubber (CR), derived from end-of-life tyres, has emerged as a promising alternative aggregate material. Although rubberised concrete is generally associated with reduced compressive strength, it has consistently been shown to improve energy absorption capacity, crack resistance, and resistance to freeze-thaw damage, making it suitable for applications subjected to dynamic or thermal loading [ 10 ].

To better understand the influence of waste-derived constituents on concrete behaviour, advanced microstructural characterisation techniques have been widely adopted. Field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) and energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) have provided detailed insight into morphology, hydration products, and interfacial transition zones in concretes modified with rubber and SCMs. These techniques reveal how pozzolanic reactions and material morphology influence porosity, bonding characteristics, and matrix continuity [ 11 ]. Additional studies have employed X-ray diffraction, multiscale analysis, and statistical approaches to compare modified concretes with conventional systems and to identify performance trends across different compositions [ 12 ].

Sustainability in the construction sector has evolved from a specialised consideration into a global priority. The buildings and construction sector is currently responsible for nearly 37% of global energy- and process-related CO₂ emissions, emphasising the urgency of adopting low-carbon and resource-efficient materials [ 13 ]. International policy frameworks, including the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals addressing infrastructure development, sustainable cities, and responsible consumption, emphasise the need for integrated sustainability strategies [ 14 ]. Initiatives such as the European Green Deal [ 15 ] and the Global Alliance for Buildings and Construction Roadmap [ 16 ] further reinforce the importance of innovation in material design and waste valorisation.

To address these gaps, the present study investigates the combined influence of CR, shredded rubber (SR), FA, SF, and MSP on mechanical performance, chloride migration, carbonation behaviour, and interfacial morphology. The experimental programme integrates mechanical and durability testing with FE-SEM and EDS to characterise microstructural development. Regression-based analysis of variance (ANOVA) is employed to quantify the influence of selected variables within the experimental matrix.

Unlike studies that examine individual materials in isolation, this work evaluates their combined behaviour within a unified experimental framework, enabling direct correlation between mechanical performance, durability response, and microstructural characteristics under consistent mix conditions. This integrated approach provides a coherent basis for interpreting multi-component interactions in sustainable concrete systems.

sections.heading: Literature review
paragraphs: Concrete’s sustainable transformation increasingly depends on substituting conventional binders and aggregates with industrial byproducts. Materials such as CR, FA, SF, MSP, and SR are widely studied for their potential to enhance durability and resource efficiency. While their individual effects are relatively well understood, the collective behaviour of such materials, particularly in multicomponent systems, remains insufficiently explored. This section synthesises recent progress while integrating key insights from foundational and emerging literature.

sections.heading: Rubberised concrete and industrial byproducts
paragraphs: Rubberised concrete commonly incorporates recycled tyre rubber in different particle forms, including CR as a partial fine aggregate replacement and SR as a partial coarse aggregate replacement. Among these forms, CR has received greater research attention because of its easier incorporation into the fine aggregate fraction and its strong influence on paste-aggregate interfacial behaviour. Rubber incorporation can improve ductility, energy absorption, and thermal insulation; however, it is commonly associated with reduced compressive strength because of weak rubber-paste bonding, lower particle stiffness, and increased porosity within the cementitious matrix [ 17 ,  18 ]. To mitigate these drawbacks, several modification strategies have been explored. Thermal treatment of rubber particles at 200 °C, when combined with fully magnetised water, has been shown to significantly enhance both compressive and tensile strength [ 19 ]. Chemical surface treatment using sodium hydroxide has also been reported to improve rubber-paste adhesion, leading to better workability, higher compressive strength, and enhanced impact resistance [ 20 ].

The thermal performance of rubberised concrete has been examined under elevated temperature exposure. Mechanical integrity has been shown to be retained at temperatures up to 300 °C, indicating adequate thermal stability [ 21 ]. Complementary observations have demonstrated reduced air permeability and acceptable strength retention in concretes incorporating waste tire extracts, supporting the suitability of rubberised concrete in applications exposed to thermal or moisture variations [ 22 ].

To counteract strength reduction associated with rubber incorporation, rubber particles are frequently combined with SCMs. The combined use of surface-modified rubber with silica fume and fly ash has been shown to increase compressive strength by 20–27% while reducing chloride ingress by more than 40%. Microstructural investigations using SEM and EDS have confirmed refined pore structures and denser interfacial transition zones, highlighting the role of SCMs in improving matrix compactness [ 11 ]. Silica fume contributes to the formation of secondary calcium silicate hydrate phases and reduces permeability [ 23 ], while the combined use of silica fume and fly ash promotes synergistic pozzolanic reactions that enhance overall performance [ 9 ].

FA, a by-product of coal combustion, has been extensively combined with rubber aggregates to improve mechanical performance while enhancing sustainability. As a pozzolanic material, fly ash reacts with calcium hydroxide to form additional cementitious phases, resulting in reduced permeability and enhanced strength development [ 24 ]. The combined incorporation of FA and CR has been shown to improve workability, durability, and resistance to freeze-thaw cycles, although mechanical performance remains sensitive to replacement levels and matrix composition [ 25 ,  26 ]. Alkali activation of fly ash using sodium silicate has further been reported to produce significant gains in compressive and tensile strength, particularly under elevated temperature conditions [ 27 ].

The influence of fly ash fineness on performance has also been investigated. Finer FA particles have been shown to significantly enhance compressive strength and reduce permeability through refinement of the interfacial transition zone. Mortar specimens incorporating the finest fly ash grade achieved compressive strength values up to 69.5 MPa at 90 days, along with reduced sorptivity and a higher normalised elastic modulus compared with control mixtures [ 28 ].

The benefits of multi-component binder systems have been further demonstrated through the use of ternary and quaternary combinations of pozzolanic materials. Such systems improve hydration efficiency and long-term durability while contributing to reductions in carbon dioxide emissions associated with cement production [ 29 ].

In addition to reactive SCMs, inert fillers such as MSP play a significant role as microfillers and water-reducing agents. Incorporation of MSP at 10% replacement has been shown to improve cohesiveness and reduce water absorption [ 7 ]. Ternary blends comprising silica fume, fly ash, and MSP have achieved compressive strengths as high as 67.3 MPa, along with superior abrasion resistance. EDS analysis has indicated Ca/Si ratios in the range of 1.6–1.8, which correlate with microstructural densification and improved load-bearing capacity [ 4 ].

The processing method of rubber particles has also been identified as a critical factor influencing performance. Cryogenic grinding has been shown to produce smoother crumb rubber particles in the size range of 50–300 μm with approximately 30% lower surface oxidation compared with ambient grinding. These characteristics improve particle compatibility with the cementitious matrix and highlight the importance of life cycle-based performance evaluation for waste-derived concrete systems [ 30 ].

Life cycle assessment studies comparing rubberised concrete produced by conventional casting and three-dimensional printing have further demonstrated environmental and performance benefits. Three-dimensionally printed mixes have been shown to achieve up to a 35% reduction in environmental footprint and a 60% reduction in material waste, while exhibiting a thermal conductivity of 0.84 W/m·K. Enhanced acoustic insulation and improved matrix compaction have also been reported, attributed to extrusion-induced densification and improved filament bonding [ 31 ].

sections.heading: Mechanical and durability performance of hybrid concrete mixes
paragraphs: Hybrid concrete systems incorporating CR, FA, SF, MSP, and SR are increasingly investigated to balance strength development with durability performance. Statistical optimisation approaches such as response surface methodology have been effectively used to design multi-component binder systems. Optimised quaternary blends comprising fly ash, silica fume, metakaolin, and zinc stearate have achieved compressive strengths exceeding 45 MPa, corrosion rates below 0.00025 mm per year, and compact gel structures confirmed through SEM observations [ 12 ].

The potential of waste-derived binders has also been demonstrated in alkali-activated systems. Binders composed of red mud and fly ash have shown a 20% increase in compressive strength and a 30% reduction in heavy metal leaching compared with ordinary Portland cement reference systems, highlighting the mechanical and environmental advantages of synergistic pozzolanic blends [ 32 ]. The inclusion of small quantities of recycled rubber, in both crumb and shredded forms, has been reported to enhance fracture toughness and energy absorption capacity while inducing only minor reductions in compressive strength [ 33 ].

The influence of rubber-induced porosity on mechanical predictability has been addressed through strength reduction models based on macro-porosity. Rubber replacement levels up to 20% have been shown to retain predictable strength performance when adequate compaction is ensured [ 34 ]. In engineered cementitious composites incorporating crumb rubber and fly ash, increased ductility has been consistently observed across varying water-to-binder ratios. However, high fly ash contents combined with low water-to-binder ratios have been reported to suppress pozzolanic reactions, leading to reduced strength development [ 35 ].

Hybrid systems combining fly ash, silica fume, and rubber have demonstrated improved mechanical behaviour when particle dispersion is well controlled, although challenges related to uniform distribution remain [ 36 ]. Durability performance under chemically aggressive environments has been addressed through the use of supplementary cementitious materials, where replacement of ordinary Portland cement with 20–60% low-calcium fly ash has been shown to significantly reduce expansion caused by sodium and magnesium sulphate exposure [ 37 ].

The applicability of response surface methodology in sustainable construction materials has been further validated through its successful application to eco-concrete systems and compressed earth blocks incorporating recycled aggregates, demonstrating the broader relevance of statistical modelling in mix optimisation [ 8 ]. Concretes containing 15–30% rubber and 7.5–15% silica fume, combined with sodium hydroxide surface treatment, have achieved enhanced microstructural packing and improved strength, despite an observed density reduction of approximately 10.5% due to the low specific gravity of rubber [ 38 ].

Additive manufacturing has further influenced the performance of rubberised concrete systems. Three-dimensionally printed rubberised concretes have exhibited lower porosity values of 0.217 compared with 0.228 for cast specimens, along with significantly higher compressive strength of 17.85 MPa compared with 4.93 MPa. Improvements in thermal and acoustic insulation have been attributed to extrusion-induced compaction and more uniform crumb rubber distribution [ 31 ]. In high-strength concrete systems, the incorporation of 10% crumb rubber has been shown to improve abrasion resistance and reduce water absorption, although a marginal reduction in compressive strength has been reported [ 39 ].

sections.heading: Microstructural and morphological characteristics
paragraphs: Microstructural refinement governs the mechanical and durability performance of crumb rubber-modified concrete systems. The combined use of clay-treated crumb rubber and silica fume has been shown to limit compressive strength reduction to approximately 0.45% relative to control mixtures. SEM analysis has revealed a significant reduction in interfacial voids and the formation of denser hydration products, indicating effective matrix refinement [ 40 ].

Chemical surface treatment of rubber particles has further been shown to enhance interfacial performance. SEM and EDS analyses have confirmed that sodium hydroxide-treated rubber improves bonding at the interfacial transition zone, reduces microcrack formation, and increases overall matrix compactness. These changes facilitate improved load transfer and reduce internal defects [ 38 ].

In three-dimensionally printed rubberised concrete, highly compact filament deposition without interlayer delamination has been observed. SEM cross-sectional imaging has demonstrated homogeneous matrix distribution and strong interlayer adhesion, contributing directly to improved mechanical integrity and enhanced thermal and acoustic insulation properties [ 31 ].

In ternary binder systems, the formation of dense gel phases and strong calcium-silicon-aluminium bonding has been attributed to optimised pozzolan-filler synergy. These microstructural characteristics are directly associated with enhanced compressive strength and improved abrasion resistance [ 4 ]. The fineness of fly ash has also been shown to play a critical role in microstructural development, particularly in mortar systems where the interfacial transition zone constitutes a larger proportion of the matrix. Finer fly ash has been reported to significantly improve the oxygen permeability index and elastic modulus through refinement of the interfacial transition zone and reduced pore connectivity [ 28 ].

sections.heading: Research gaps and study rationale
paragraphs: Although extensive research has been conducted on concrete incorporating industrial byproducts and waste-derived materials, several important gaps remain. First, the majority of published studies have examined the individual effects of CR, FA, SF, MSP, or SR in isolation. As a result, limited understanding exists regarding the combined behaviour of these materials when used together in multi-component binder and aggregate systems under consistent experimental conditions.

Second, relatively few investigations have simultaneously evaluated mechanical performance, durability-related properties such as chloride ingress and water absorption, and microstructural characteristics using the same specimen sets. This fragmented approach restricts the ability to establish clear links between material composition, performance trends, and underlying mechanisms governing durability and strength development.

Third, although advanced characterisation techniques such as scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) are widely available, they are often applied selectively to a limited number of mixtures rather than systematically across representative mix categories. Consequently, correlations between morphological features, interfacial transition zone characteristics, and corresponding mechanical or durability responses remain incomplete.

Fourth, while statistical and data-driven approaches including analysis of variance, response surface methods, and machine learning have demonstrated potential in concrete research, their application to multi-component sustainable concrete systems remains limited. In many cases, such methods are used either to screen dominant variables or to model specific material classes, rather than to support integrated interpretation of experimental trends within complex mixture systems [ 41 ].

In light of these gaps, the present study investigates the combined influence of CR, SR, FA, SF, and MSP on the mechanical performance, durability indicators, and microstructural characteristics of concrete. The experimental programme evaluates compressive strength, chloride migration, water absorption, carbonation depth, and interfacial morphology within a consistent testing framework. Regression-based ANOVA is employed to quantify the influence of selected variables within the experimental matrix.

Unlike approaches that address individual properties or materials in isolation, this study integrates mechanical, durability, and microstructural evaluation within a unified experimental design, enabling direct interpretation of material interactions under consistent mix conditions.

The study is structured as a comparative investigation rather than a global optimisation exercise, with the objective of clarifying performance trends in multi-component sustainable concrete systems. An overview of the experimental framework is presented in Fig.  1 .

sections.heading: Materials and analysis
paragraphs: This section describes the constituent materials, testing equipment, mix design considerations, and experimental procedures adopted to evaluate the performance of concrete modified with supplementary cementitious materials and rubber-based aggregates.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: The materials used in this study were selected to ensure compliance with relevant Indian standards and to represent locally available resources suitable for sustainable concrete production. Ordinary Portland Cement (OPC) of 53 grade, manufactured by Ultratech Cement Ltd., Bhopal, was used as the primary binder and conformed to the requirements of IS 12,269 [ 42 ]. Natural river sand, classified as Zone II fine aggregate with a fineness modulus of 2.87, was sourced from the Narmada River and met the specifications of IS 383 [ 43 ]. Coarse aggregates consisted of crushed basalt stones of 10 mm and 20 mm nominal sizes, obtained from Dhakad Traders, Bhopal. The selection and reporting of aggregate properties follow codal provisions and are consistent with recent studies on alternative aggregates and steel slag-based concrete systems [ 44 ,  45 – 46 ].

MSP, generated as a byproduct during stone cutting and polishing operations, was collected from Taj Stone Company, Bhopal. The wet slurry was air-dried under ambient conditions and subsequently sieved to pass through a 90 μm sieve prior to use. FA was procured from the Satpura Thermal Power Station, Sarni, Madhya Pradesh, and exhibited 82% passing through a 45 μm sieve. The material complied with IS 3812 [ 47 ] and satisfied the requirements of Class F fly ash as per ASTM C618 [ 48 ].

CR and SR were sourced from Sai Tires, a local tyre recycling facility in Bhopal, India. The CR was processed and sieved to obtain a nominal particle size range of approximately 0.6–2.36 mm, corresponding to standard fine aggregate sieve limits. It exhibited a specific gravity of 1.12 and a bulk density of 560 kg/m³. The relatively fine gradation and high surface area of CR (fineness modulus of 4.48) made it suitable for partial replacement of natural fine aggregate in the concrete mixtures. Prior to incorporation, the recycled rubber fractions were screened to the specified size ranges to ensure consistent gradation and compatibility with the corresponding aggregate fractions, following preparation practices commonly adopted for recycled materials in cementitious composites [ 49 ,  50 ].

SR, used as a partial substitute for coarse aggregate, consisted of particles in the size range of 4.75–19 mm, with a specific gravity of 1.18 and a bulk density of 1280 kg/m³. The particles were angular in shape and free from visible metallic contaminants. These physical characteristics fall within the limits specified for Type A tyre-derived aggregates in ASTM D6270 [ 51 ], supporting their suitability for use in concrete applications where recycled aggregates are permitted.

SF, supplied by Metro Chemicals, Bhopal, satisfied the requirements of IS 15,388 [ 52 ] and ASTM C1240 [ 53 ]. The material consisted of extremely fine particles, with more than 99% passing the 45 μm sieve.

All concrete mixes were prepared using potable tap water with a neutral pH of approximately 7. A polycarboxylate ether (PCE)-based high-range water-reducing admixture (HRWR), SikaPlast-5202 NS, was used to regulate workability and improve particle dispersion. The admixture had a minimum pH of 6 and was used in accordance with the manufacturer’s recommendations [ 54 ].

sections.heading: Equipment
paragraphs: A range of standard laboratory instruments was employed to determine material properties and to conduct mechanical and microstructural investigations. Cement testing equipment supplied by Zeal International, New Delhi, India, was used to measure specific gravity using a Le Chatelier flask, while standard consistency and setting times were determined using Vicat’s apparatus. Soundness was assessed using the Le Chatelier method in accordance with applicable Indian standards [ 55 ,  56 ,  57 – 58 ]. These procedures are broadly consistent with international testing practices, including ASTM C187 [ 59 ] and ASTM C191 [ 60 ], for evaluating cement water demand and setting characteristics.

Microstructural and elemental analyses were carried out at the Sophisticated Instrumentation Facility (SIF), BITS Pilani (Pilani Campus). A Thermo Fisher Scientific (FEI) Apreo S model FE-SEM was used to obtain high-resolution images of hardened concrete specimens, allowing detailed examination of hydration products, interfacial transition zones, and overall matrix morphology. Elemental composition and spatial distribution were analysed using an OXFORD Instruments X-Max N  EDS system coupled with the FE-SEM. Prior to imaging, specimens were coated with a thin gold layer using a Quorum Technologies Q150T ES sputter coater to ensure adequate electrical conductivity.

Fresh concrete workability was evaluated using a standard slump cone apparatus manufactured by Zeal International. Slump tests were conducted in accordance with IS 1199 [ 61 ], which is comparable in test procedure and cone geometry to ASTM C143/C143M [ 62 ] and EN 12350-2 [ 63 ]. Compressive strength tests on cube and cylindrical specimens were performed using a 2000 kN capacity compression testing machine supplied by Enkay Enterprises, New Delhi, India. Flexural strength of beam specimens was measured using a dedicated 100 kN flexural testing machine under third-point loading conditions.

sections.heading: Mix proportions
paragraphs: The concrete mix design was formulated to evaluate the individual and combined effects of industrial byproducts and rubber-based aggregate modifications on the mechanical, durability, and microstructural performance of concrete. OPC of 53 grade was used as the primary binder. River sand served as the fine aggregate, while crushed basalt aggregates of 20 mm and 10 mm nominal sizes were blended in a fixed 60:40 ratio to form the coarse aggregate skeleton. To ensure comparability among mixtures, the water-to-binder (w/b) ratio was maintained constant at 0.35 for all mixes.

Fresh concrete workability was targeted at a slump of 160 ± 20 mm to ensure adequate placement and compaction, particularly for mixtures incorporating rubberised aggregates. A PCE-based HRWR was used to regulate workability and improve particle dispersion. Because SCMs and rubber particles differ in morphology, surface texture, and interaction with the cementitious matrix, the HRWR dosage was adjusted within a controlled range of 0.8–1.4% by mass of total binder while keeping the w/b ratio constant. This approach allowed the effects of material substitution to be evaluated without introducing additional variation due to changes in water content.

The reference mixture, designated C0F0A0, consisted of 100% OPC with natural fine and coarse aggregates and served as the baseline for comparison. In the first phase, binder-level modifications were introduced by partially replacing OPC with FA, SF, and MSP at fixed replacement levels of 15%, 5%, and 10% by weight of cement, respectively. These materials were used individually and in combination to produce mixes C1F0A0 to C4F0A0, while the aggregate composition was kept unchanged. The selected SCM replacement levels were adopted based on prior experimental studies reporting acceptable mechanical and durability performance for similar ternary binder systems [ 4 ].

In the second phase, CR was incorporated as a 12.5% replacement of river sand by volume, producing the parallel series C0F1A0 to C4F1A0 with the same binder combinations as the first phase. In the third phase, SR was used as a 10% replacement of crushed stone aggregate by volume, resulting in mixes C0F0A1 to C4F0A1 without CR and C0F1A1 to C4F1A1 with both CR and SR. The selected rubber replacement levels were kept moderate, consistent with commonly adopted ranges in rubberised concrete [ 10 ], to enable comparative performance evaluation rather than mix-design optimisation.

In total, twenty concrete mixtures were produced. The stepwise mix design enabled direct comparison of the effects of binder composition, fine aggregate replacement, coarse aggregate replacement, and their combined interactions. In the mix nomenclature, ‘C’ denotes the cementitious system, ‘F’ indicates the fine aggregate condition, representing the absence or presence of CR, and ‘A’ represents the coarse aggregate condition, representing the absence or presence of SR. sections.heading: Experimental design
paragraphs: The experimental programme was designed to examine the influence of selected industrial byproducts and rubber-based aggregate modifications on the fresh, mechanical, durability, and microstructural properties of concrete. A reference mix, designated C0F0A0, was prepared in accordance with IS 456 [ 64 ] using 100% OPC and natural fine and coarse aggregates. This reference mixture served as a code-compliant reference baseline, against which the effects of subsequent material substitutions were evaluated. The overall experimental strategy, involving systematic variation of binder and aggregate constituents while maintaining key mix parameters constant, is consistent with approaches adopted in recent studies on alternative aggregate and waste-modified concrete systems [ 65 ,  66 ].

SCMs, including FA, SF, and MSP, were incorporated as partial replacements of cement to examine their individual and combined influence on concrete performance. CR and SR were introduced as partial replacements of fine and coarse aggregates, respectively, to assess their effect on mechanical behaviour and durability-related characteristics. Each material was selected based on its documented functional contribution. FA and SF were used for their pozzolanic reactivity and potential to enhance matrix densification through secondary hydration, while MSP was incorporated primarily for its filler effect and its influence on pore refinement. CR and SR were included to evaluate their influence on flexural response, crack-development behaviour, and deformability-related performance, particularly when combined with SCMs.

The experimental programme focused on evaluating key performance indicators, including compressive strength (CS), split tensile strength (TS), flexural strength (FS), and workability. Compressive and split tensile strengths were determined using 150 mm cube specimens and 150 × 300 mm cylindrical specimens, respectively, in accordance with IS 516 [ 67 ] and IS 5816 [ 68 ]. These test procedures are comparable in configuration and loading conditions to ASTM C39/C39M [ 69 ], ASTM C496/C496M [ 70 ], EN 12390-3 [ 71 ], and EN 12390-6 [ 72 ]. Flexural strength was measured on 500 × 100 × 100 mm beam specimens under third-point loading as specified in IS 516, following a procedure similar to ASTM C78/C78M [ 73 ] and EN 12390-5 [ 74 ]. Fresh concrete workability was assessed using the slump cone test in accordance with IS 1199, which is comparable to ASTM C143/C143M and EN 12350-2.

Durability-related properties were evaluated through water absorption and permeable void measurements in accordance with ASTM C642 [ 75 ], which provides an index of absorption capacity and accessible pore volume in hardened concrete. This assessment is consistent in purpose with BS 1881 − 122:2011 + A1:2020 [ 76 ], which specifies a standard method for determining water absorption in hardened concrete specimens. Resistance to chloride ingress was assessed using the Rapid Chloride Migration Test (RCMT) in accordance with NT Build 492 [ 77 ], a widely adopted procedure for evaluating chloride transport in concrete. Although ASTM C1202 [ 78 ] is commonly used to assess resistance to chloride ion penetration based on charge passed, NT Build 492 was adopted in the present study because it directly provides a chloride migration coefficient. Carbonation depth was measured after accelerated exposure in a CO₂ chamber at a concentration of 4%, using a procedure aligned with the intent of EN 13,295 [ 79 ] for carbonation resistance assessment. All specimens were cast in steel moulds and cured at 27 ± 2 °C and 95% relative humidity. Each test result represents the average of three specimens.

Microstructural characterisation was carried out using FE-SEM and EDS to examine hydration products, interfacial transition zones, and elemental distribution within selected representative mixtures. These observations were used to support interpretation of mechanical and durability trends rather than to establish quantitative microstructural metrics.

To support interpretation of the experimental results, regression-based ANOVA was employed to examine the influence of selected variables, specifically FA and CR, on strength-related responses within the experimental matrix. The statistical analysis was used to identify dominant effects and general trends rather than to perform global optimisation or comprehensive interaction modelling.

sections.heading: Results and discussion
paragraphs: This section presents the experimental findings from the particle size distribution (PSD) analysis, fresh concrete workability, mechanical strength evaluation, durability assessment, microstructural characterisation, and statistical interpretation of the modified concrete mixtures. The results are discussed with reference to the effects of binder composition, CR and SR incorporation, and their combined influence on concrete performance. Regression-based ANOVA is further used to interpret the relative influence of selected variables on strength-related responses.

sections.heading: Particle size
paragraphs: The PSD of the constituent materials influences packing density, surface area, reactivity, and particle compatibility, all of which affect the fresh and hardened properties of concrete. In this study, PSD analysis was conducted for CR, MSP, SF, FA, and OPC to understand their relative fineness and blending behaviour within the cementitious matrix.

As shown in Fig.  2 , SF exhibited the finest particle size distribution, followed by FA and MSP. These finer materials can contribute to matrix refinement through filler action and pozzolanic reaction, thereby improving particle packing and reducing pore connectivity. OPC showed a moderate particle size profile typical of 53-grade cement. In contrast, CR exhibited a broader and coarser size range, reflecting its aggregate-like role rather than binder-like behaviour. The coarser and more deformable nature of CR can contribute to ductility and energy absorption, but may also interrupt matrix continuity and weaken the rubber-paste interface if not balanced by adequate binder refinement. The PSD results therefore provide a useful basis for interpreting the subsequent workability, strength, durability, and microstructural trends.
Fig. 2 Particle size distribution curve for CR, MSP, SF, FA, and OPC

sections.heading: Workability Test on Fresh Concrete
paragraphs: The workability of fresh concrete was evaluated for all twenty mixtures using the standard slump cone test. The measured slump values reflect the combined influence of binder composition, CR incorporation, SR incorporation, and HRWR dosage on fresh-state behaviour. Figure  3  presents the slump results for the investigated mixes.

The reference mix C0F0A0, prepared with OPC and natural aggregates, exhibited a slump of 135 mm, indicating satisfactory workability. Partial replacement of cement with individual SCMs produced a modest increase in slump. The incorporation of 15% FA in C1F0A0, 5% SF in C2F0A0, and 10% MSP in C3F0A0 improved workability relative to the reference mix. This improvement can be attributed to changes in paste rheology and particle dispersion. In particular, the spherical morphology of FA and the fine filler effect of MSP can enhance internal lubrication and improve flowability.

Mixtures containing CR as a partial replacement of fine aggregate generally showed a slight reduction in slump compared with corresponding mixes without CR. This reduction is mainly associated with the irregular shape, rough surface texture, and low stiffness of rubber particles, which increase internal friction and may increase entrapped air content. Since rubber has limited water absorption compared with natural aggregates, the reduction in flowability is more reasonably linked to particle morphology and interfacial effects than to absorption of mixing water.

The highest slump values, 172 mm and 179 mm, were observed for C3F0A1 and C4F0A1, respectively. These mixes contained SR as a partial replacement of coarse aggregate and included MSP, while C4F0A1 also incorporated the combined FA-SF-MSP binder system. The improved flow in these mixtures may be attributed to better paste dispersion, reduced interparticle friction from fine mineral additions, and the elastic response of SR particles, which facilitated movement within the fresh mix without visibly compromising cohesion.

The slump results indicate that workability was effectively controlled across the investigated mixtures by maintaining a constant w/b ratio and adjusting HRWR dosage within the selected range. This allowed the effects of SCMs and rubberised aggregates on fresh concrete behaviour to be evaluated without introducing additional variation from uncontrolled water-content changes.
Fig. 3 Slump values of fresh concrete mixes with varying binder and aggregate modifications

sections.heading: Mechanical properties
paragraphs: To evaluate the mechanical performance of the modified concrete mixes, compressive strength, split tensile strength, and flexural strength were measured at curing ages of 7, 14, 28, and 90 days. For conciseness, these parameters are referred to as CS, TS, and FS, respectively, in the comparative and statistical discussion. The corresponding results are presented in Figs.  4  and  5 , and  6 .

As shown in Fig.  4 , the reference mix C0F0A0 exhibited the highest compressive strength at all curing ages, reflecting the dense and continuous matrix formed by OPC and natural aggregates. The incorporation of CR generally reduced compressive strength, particularly in mixes without SCMs, such as C0F1A0. This reduction can be attributed to the hydrophobic and deformable nature of rubber particles, weak rubber-paste bonding, and the presence of low-stiffness inclusions that interrupt stress transfer within the cementitious matrix [ 80 ,  81 – 82 ]. Recent mesoscale evidence supports this interpretation, indicating that rubber content is a dominant factor controlling strength reduction and that rubber particles may behave partly as pore-like inclusions within the cementitious skeleton [ 83 ].
Fig. 4 Compressive strength (MPa) of mixes

When CR was combined with FA or SF, partial recovery in compressive strength was observed. Mixes such as C1F1A0 and C2F1A0 showed higher strength than the rubber-only mix C0F1A0, indicating that pozzolanic reactions and filler effects contributed to matrix densification and secondary calcium silicate hydrate (C-S-H) formation. Similar improvements associated with continued FA hydration and pore refinement have also been reported in previous studies [ 84 ]. The use of industrial ash residues in concrete also supports sustainable material management by promoting the utilisation of byproducts in cementitious systems [ 85 ].

Although SCM incorporation did not fully restore the strength to that of the control mix, it moderated the strength loss caused by rubber inclusion. This behaviour is consistent with recent studies on CR concrete containing SCMs, where replacement of natural sand with 10–20% CR reduced compressive strength by up to 25.4%, while the incorporation of SF and rice husk ash mitigated this reduction through improved particle packing and additional hydration products observed through FE-SEM [ 86 ]. Similarly, optimisation-based work on SF-modified rubberised concrete reported that a combination of 15% SF, 2.5% fine rubber, and 2.5% coarse rubber improved 28-day compressive strength, 56-day compressive strength, and 28-day flexural strength by 4.55%, 4.92%, and 5.34%, respectively, indicating that controlled rubber contents combined with reactive fines can produce a more balanced mechanical response [ 87 ].

The split tensile strength results, presented in Fig.  5 , followed a trend broadly similar to compressive strength. Rubber-containing mixes generally showed lower TS because of reduced interfacial bonding and increased strain localisation around rubber particles. However, binary and ternary binder systems incorporating SCMs showed comparatively improved tensile performance. In particular, mixes containing 5% SF, such as C2F0A1 and C2F1A0, showed better resistance to tensile cracking. This improvement can be attributed to pore refinement, enhanced matrix continuity, and improved stress distribution within the cementitious matrix, which collectively delay crack initiation and propagation.
Fig. 5 Split tensile strength (MPa) of mixes

The flexural strength results, presented in Fig.  6 , showed a more mix-dependent response than compressive and split tensile strength. Unlike the clearer reduction observed in compressive and split tensile behaviour, rubber incorporation did not produce a uniform decrease in FS. At 28 days, the control mix C0F0A0 achieved an FS of 14.00 MPa, whereas rubber-containing mixes such as C0F1A0, C0F0A1, and C0F1A1 reached 15.66 MPa, 16.12 MPa, and 15.50 MPa, respectively. This indicates that, although rubber particles reduce stiffness and weaken the rubber-paste interface, their deformable nature can contribute to crack deflection, strain accommodation, and delayed crack localisation under flexural loading.

The flexural response was therefore governed by the combined effects of rubber type, binder composition, and matrix continuity rather than by rubber content alone. Mixes incorporating SF, such as C2F1A0 and C2F0A1, retained comparatively high flexural strength, indicating that pore refinement and improved hydration product continuity helped maintain load transfer across the tensile zone. In contrast, mixes with higher binder replacement or limited reactive refinement showed lower flexural values, suggesting that filler or dilution effects may reduce stress-transfer efficiency when not balanced by sufficient matrix densification.

Distinct differences in failure behaviour were also observed during flexural testing. The control mix C0F0A0 typically exhibited sudden and brittle failure, characterised by rapid propagation of a single dominant crack initiating at the tensile face. In contrast, rubberised mixes showed more gradual crack development, with visible crack deflection and distributed cracking before failure. This response is attributed to the deformable nature of rubber particles, which locally accommodate strain and delay crack localisation. Although this behaviour does not necessarily indicate higher stiffness or tensile strength, it reflects a shift toward a less brittle flexural response in rubber-containing mixes. Comparable changes in flexural cracking behaviour and ductility enhancement due to rubber inclusion have been documented in earlier studies on rubberised concrete systems [ 88 ].

Since fracture energy and toughness were not directly measured, the observed changes in cracking behaviour are interpreted qualitatively. Nevertheless, these observations help explain why some rubberised mixes retained or improved flexural strength despite reductions in compressive and split tensile strength.
Fig. 6 Flexural strength (MPa) of mixes

the mechanical results indicate that CR incorporation reduced compressive and split tensile strength, while the flexural response was more strongly governed by rubber type, binder composition, and matrix continuity. The strength loss associated with rubber inclusion was moderated by reactive SCMs, particularly in mixes where matrix densification and hydration product continuity improved stress transfer. Among the investigated mixtures, C2F1A0 showed a favourable balance between strength retention and material sustainability, indicating potential suitability for non-structural and lightly loaded applications. Similar trends have been reported for optimised CR-FA systems, where mechanically stable concrete with enhanced ductility and improved crack control has been achieved [ 10 ].

sections.heading: Durability properties
paragraphs: The long-term performance of concrete under aggressive environmental exposure is strongly influenced by its resistance to fluid ingress, ionic transport, and carbonation. In this study, durability was evaluated through water absorption, chloride migration, and carbonation depth for all twenty concrete mixtures. The corresponding results are presented in Figs.  7  and  8 , and  9 .

Figure  7  presents the water absorption results of the investigated mixes. The reference mix C0F0A0 exhibited relatively low water absorption, reflecting the compact matrix formed by OPC and natural aggregates. In contrast, mixes incorporating CR without effective binder modification, such as C0F1A0 and C0F1A1, showed increased absorption. This behaviour can be attributed to the irregular morphology, hydrophobic surface characteristics, and deformable nature of rubber particles, which weaken the rubber-paste interface and introduce localised voids around the aggregate phase.

The incorporation of SCMs, particularly SF and MSP, reduced water uptake by improving matrix compactness and limiting connected capillary pores. In SF-modified mixes such as C2F0A0, the reduction in absorption is mainly associated with pozzolanic reaction, secondary C-S-H formation, and refinement of the pore structure. In MSP-containing mixes such as C3F0A0, the improvement is more closely related to filler action and pore blocking. These mechanisms collectively reduced accessible porosity and improved resistance to fluid ingress, consistent with previous findings on SCM-modified concrete systems [ 89 ,  90 ].
Fig. 7 Water absorption results of concrete mixes

As shown in Fig.  8 , chloride migration coefficients varied with binder composition and rubber incorporation. OPC-only and rubberised mixes without effective binder refinement showed higher chloride migration, indicating the presence of more connected transport pathways. These pathways are associated with capillary porosity and weak rubber-paste interfacial zones, which can facilitate ionic movement through the concrete matrix.

When CR was combined with SCMs, especially in mixes C2F1A0 and C2F1A1, chloride resistance improved markedly. SF played a major role in this improvement because of its ultrafine particle size and high pozzolanic reactivity, which promote C-S-H formation, refine the pore network, and restrict chloride ion movement. This trend agrees with recent work on multi-blended CR concrete systems, where the combined incorporation of CR, SF, rice husk ash, copper slag, and steel slag improved strength and durability-related performance, including chloride resistance, through matrix densification and microstructural refinement [ 91 ]. Although the binder and aggregate combinations differ from the FA-SF-MSP system used in the present study, both sets of results indicate that rubber-induced transport vulnerability can be moderated when SCMs and industrial byproducts refine the cementitious matrix.
Fig. 8 Chloride migration results of the concrete mixes after 28 days

The carbonation depth results, presented in Fig.  9 , further clarify the durability response of the investigated mixes. Carbonation was not governed by rubber incorporation alone, but by the combined influence of rubber-paste interfacial zones, matrix compactness, and binder-induced pore refinement. Mixes with less effective matrix refinement, such as C0F0A0, C3F0A0, and C3F0A1, showed comparatively higher carbonation depths, indicating greater CO₂ ingress through a more connected pore structure.

Similar mechanisms linking carbonation susceptibility to interconnected pores, weak interfacial zones, and reduced buffering capacity have been reported in recent durability-focused studies on modified CR concrete [ 92 ]. In contrast, mixes incorporating SF or ternary binder combinations showed reduced carbonation depths where matrix densification and improved pore discontinuity were achieved. Among the investigated mixtures, SF-containing mixes generally exhibited favourable carbonation resistance, reflecting the role of SF in reducing transport pathways and improving matrix compactness.
Fig. 9 Carbonation results of the concrete mixes

The durability results indicate that rubber incorporation without adequate binder refinement can increase water absorption, chloride migration, and carbonation susceptibility because of weaker interfacial zones and greater transport connectivity. However, these adverse effects were moderated through the incorporation of suitable SCMs. Selected combinations of CR with SF and MSP improved resistance to water ingress, chloride transport, and carbonation by refining the cementitious matrix and reducing connected pore networks. While SF-based mixes exhibited the best absolute durability performance, ternary binder systems remain important from a sustainability and material-utilisation perspective because they enable broader waste valorisation while maintaining acceptable durability for non-structural and lightly loaded applications. These trends are consistent with earlier studies highlighting the role of finely divided pozzolanic materials in reducing transport-driven deterioration mechanisms [ 29 ].

sections.heading: Microstructural and Morphological Characterisation
paragraphs: Microstructural characterisation was undertaken to examine the influence of CR, SR, and SCMs on the internal structure of concrete. The analysis focused on hydration products, pore morphology, and interfacial transition zone (ITZ) characteristics in selected representative mixes. FE-SEM and EDS were used to support interpretation of the mechanical and durability trends observed in the experimental programme. The observations are therefore presented as mechanistic support rather than as a comprehensive or statistically generalised assessment across all mixtures.

From the twenty mixes investigated, two representative mixtures were selected for detailed microstructural examination. The control mix C0F0A0, consisting of OPC and natural aggregates, was selected as the reference system. The fully modified mix C4F1A1, incorporating FA, SF, MSP, CR, and SR, was selected to represent the highest level of material substitution within the experimental matrix. Although this mix showed lower strength than the control, its performance remained within acceptable limits for non-structural and durability-sensitive applications. The comparison between these two mixes was intended to provide a qualitative contrast between conventional and highly modified systems.

sections.heading: Morphology via FE-SEM
paragraphs: FE-SEM analysis was carried out to examine hydration product morphology, matrix continuity, and ITZ characteristics in the selected representative mixes. The purpose of this analysis was to support interpretation of mechanical and durability behaviour through visual comparison of conventional and highly modified systems.

The control mix C0F0A0 exhibited a comparatively heterogeneous microstructure. The FE-SEM image showed loosely packed hydration products, clearly distinguishable portlandite crystals, and regions of discontinuous gel formation. The ITZ appeared relatively porous and irregular, with visible microcracks and weakly bonded regions. These features are consistent with a hydration system governed primarily by OPC, where limited secondary gel formation occurs and pore refinement remains relatively limited. Such morphology can contribute to greater transport susceptibility and lower resistance to ingress-related durability mechanisms. The representative micrograph of this mix is shown in Fig.  10 .
Fig. 10 FE-SEM micrograph of conventional mix (C0F0A0)

In contrast, the modified mix C4F1A1 displayed a denser and more cohesive matrix. The microstructure was characterised by a greater prevalence of gel-rich regions and a more continuous cementitious phase. The ITZ appeared comparatively refined, with improved contact between the paste and surrounding inclusions. Localised voids associated with rubber particles were visible; however, the surrounding matrix showed improved cohesion and reduced microcracking compared with the control mix. The combined incorporation of FA, SF, and MSP likely contributed to secondary hydration, filler action, improved particle packing, and matrix densification. These mechanisms partially offset the discontinuities introduced by CR and SR and help explain the improved durability response observed in the modified mixes. The representative FE-SEM image of this mix is presented in Fig.  11 .
Fig. 11 FE-SEM micrograph of rubberised mix (C4F1A1)

sections.heading: Elemental Mapping via EDS
paragraphs: EDS analysis was performed to qualitatively examine the distribution of key elements associated with cement hydration and pozzolanic reactions, particularly calcium (Ca), silicon (Si), aluminium (Al), and oxygen (O). The EDS spectrum of the control mix C0F0A0 was characterised by dominant Ca and O peaks, indicating a matrix primarily governed by portlandite-rich hydration products. The Si and Al signals were comparatively weaker and less uniformly distributed, suggesting limited contribution from secondary gel formation. The corresponding EDS spectrum is presented in Fig.  12 .
Fig. 12 EDS spectrum of conventional concrete (C0F0A0)

In contrast, the modified mix C4F1A1 exhibited comparatively higher and more uniformly distributed Si and Al intensities relative to Ca. This elemental distribution indicates enhanced pozzolanic activity and the formation of secondary C-S-H and calcium aluminosilicate hydrate (C-A-S-H) type phases. The relative reduction in Ca dominance, inferred from the spectral trends, is consistent with a more refined hydration matrix. Minor traces of sulphur and metallic elements associated with rubber particles were detected as secondary inclusions, but these did not appear to disrupt the continuity of the primary cementitious phases. The EDS spectrum of this mix is shown in Fig.  13 .
Fig. 13 EDS spectrum of rubberised mix (C4F1A1)

The observed elemental trends support the improved durability performance of SCM-modified mixes by indicating greater matrix refinement and more uniform hydration product development. However, these observations do not fully offset the mechanical limitations associated with rubber incorporation and are therefore interpreted as supportive rather than definitive evidence.

sections.heading: Correlation with performance
paragraphs: The microstructural observations provide qualitative support for the mechanical and durability trends observed experimentally. The control mix C0F0A0 achieved higher compressive and split tensile strength; however, FE-SEM imaging revealed microcracking, portlandite agglomeration, and limited ITZ refinement, while EDS confirmed a Ca-rich matrix with comparatively lower Si and Al participation. These features help explain why the control mix did not exhibit the same level of matrix refinement observed in selected SCM-modified mixes, particularly with respect to resistance against fluid ingress and carbonation.

The modified mix C4F1A1 exhibited improved matrix refinement and a more homogeneous hydration structure, as indicated by gel-rich morphology and reduced Ca dominance relative to Si in the EDS response. These characteristics are consistent with the improved durability performance observed in terms of reduced chloride ingress and carbonation depth. At the same time, the presence of CR and SR introduced compliant inclusions and localised voids, which adversely affected stress transfer and resulted in reduced strength relative to the control mix.

The microstructural analysis highlights the dual influence of rubber incorporation in multi-component concrete systems. While SCMs enhanced matrix refinement and durability by improving pore structure and hydration product continuity, their beneficial effects only partially compensated for the mechanical penalties associated with rubber aggregates. These findings emphasise the need for balanced material selection when targeting sustainability improvements alongside acceptable mechanical performance.

sections.heading: Regression-based ANOVA
paragraphs: The experimental results were analysed using regression-based ANOVA following the framework of Snedecor and Cochran [ 93 ], with a 95% confidence level ( p  < 0.05). The analysis was used to examine the influence of FA and CR on the mechanical behaviour of concrete within the defined experimental matrix.

SF, MSP, and SR were incorporated at fixed replacement levels or appeared only in specific ternary and quaternary combinations. These constituents were therefore not treated as independent continuous variables in the regression formulation. Their influence was interpreted through comparative experimental trends supported by representative microstructural observations, consistent with regression-based analyses of multi-component concrete systems where fixed-level modifiers are excluded to preserve interpretability [ 94 ].

The study was structured as a controlled comparative investigation with a limited number of mix configurations to evaluate combined material effects. Within this framework, regression analysis was employed to support interpretation of dominant trends rather than to establish generalised predictive models or full multivariate optimisation. Accordingly, the results are interpreted within the defined experimental domain.

The regression analysis was applied to compressive strength, split tensile strength, and flexural strength. In the regression formulation, C and D denote the coded statistical factors representing FA and CR, respectively, and should not be confused with the mix-label notation used to identify binder and aggregate combinations. The model includes the main effects of FA (C) and CR (D), their interaction term (CD), and quadratic terms (C² and D²) to capture nonlinear behaviour. A categorical variable, designated as Pattern, represents systematic differences among mix series arising from combined binder and aggregate configurations.

CR exhibited a strong negative linear influence across all strength models, consistent with reduced stress transfer, weaker rubber-paste bonding, and increased deformability. FA showed a comparatively weaker independent contribution within the tested range, while the categorical Pattern variable captured the combined effects of fixed-level constituents, including SF, MSP, and SR (Table  3 ).

Table 3 Summary of regression-based ANOVA results for strength properties Properties Source Degree of freedom F-value p -value Significance Compressive strength Pattern 7 83.23 < 0.0001 Significant FA (C) 1 1.95 0.2001 Not significant CR (D) 1 700.35 < 0.0001 Significant CD 1 0.013 0.9120 Not significant C 2 1 3.02 0.1204 Not significant D 2 1 15.22 0.0045 Significant Tensile strength Pattern 7 21.41 0.0001 Significant FA (C) 1 3.12 0.1153 Not significant CR (D) 1 138.72 < 0.0001 Significant CD 1 5.15 0.0529 Not significant C 2 1 9.83 0.0139 Significant D 2 1 2.01 0.1940 Not significant Flexural strength Pattern 7 5.73 0.0126 Significant FA (C) 1 1.45 0.2629 Not significant CR (D) 1 31.25 0.0005 Significant CD 1 8.43 0.0198 Significant C 2 1 0.72 0.4208 Not significant D 2 1 0.10 0.7599 Not significant Significance was evaluated at a 95% confidence level. Terms with  p  < 0.05 were considered statistically significant

For the full fitted regression models, including the categorical Pattern term, the coefficients of determination (R²) were 0.81 for compressive strength, 0.91 for split tensile strength, and 0.97 for flexural strength. These values indicate that the models captured the principal strength trends within the tested experimental domain. The ANOVA results further indicate that CR was the most influential variable affecting strength response, as CR (D) was statistically significant for compressive, split tensile, and flexural strength. This confirms that rubber incorporation strongly modifies stress transfer within the concrete matrix. The Pattern variable was also significant for all three strength parameters, indicating that fixed-level constituents such as SF, MSP, and SR influenced strength through combined binder and aggregate configurations.

The significance of D² for compressive strength, C² for split tensile strength, and CD for flexural strength indicates that nonlinear and interaction effects were response-specific rather than uniform across all strength parameters. Given the limited dataset and the inclusion of categorical effects, the R² values should not be interpreted as measures of the independent predictive strength of individual variables [ 95 ]. This cautious interpretation is consistent with recent data-driven work on recycled rubber aggregate concrete, where machine-learning models developed from 369 experimental samples showed high predictive accuracy and identified rubberised aggregate content as the most influential negative factor affecting compressive strength [ 96 ].

When considered alongside the experimental results and microstructural observations, the regression-based ANOVA provides a consistent interpretation of the behaviour of rubberised concrete incorporating SCMs. The findings are therefore presented as performance trends within a constrained experimental framework. Their applicability should be interpreted within the defined parameter space and modelling assumptions, highlighting the importance of balanced mix design and cautious generalisation when evaluating multi-component sustainable concrete systems, consistent with recent experimental and analytical studies on waste-modified concretes [ 97 ,  98 ,  99 – 100 ].

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This study examined twenty concrete mixtures incorporating CR, SR, FA, SF, and MSP to evaluate the combined effects of rubber aggregates and SCMs on mechanical performance, durability, microstructure, and statistical response. Based on the experimental results, FE-SEM and EDS observations, and regression-based ANOVA, the following conclusions are drawn:

The incorporation of CR reduced the strength response of concrete, particularly compressive and split tensile strength, because of weak rubber-paste adhesion, lower particle stiffness, and increased local deformability within the cementitious matrix. The flexural response was more dependent on the combined rubber-binder configuration and was strongly influenced by interfacial bonding, matrix continuity, and crack-deflection behaviour. Compared with corresponding rubber-modified reference mixtures, selected SCM-modified mixes showed strength recovery of up to 12% in compressive strength, 8% in split tensile strength, and 10% in flexural strength, mainly due to matrix densification and improved hydration product continuity.

Durability performance was governed by the balance between rubber-induced transport pathways and SCM-induced pore refinement. Rubber-containing mixtures without adequate binder modification showed greater susceptibility to water absorption, chloride migration, and carbonation. In contrast, SF- and MSP-modified mixes showed approximately 15–20% reduction in water absorption and chloride migration indicators, reflecting improved particle packing, reduced connected porosity, and a denser cementitious matrix.

The microstructural observations supported the mechanical and durability trends. The control mix showed portlandite-rich regions, microcracking, and a comparatively discontinuous ITZ. SCM-modified rubberised mixes showed more gel-rich morphology, improved matrix continuity, and more uniform elemental distribution. These observations indicate that FA, SF, and MSP improved the internal structure of the matrix, although the stress-transfer limitations associated with rubber inclusion were not fully eliminated.

Regression-based ANOVA identified CR content as the dominant factor influencing strength response within the tested experimental domain. The Pattern variable was also significant for compressive, split tensile, and flexural strength, confirming that fixed-level constituents such as SF, MSP, and SR affected the strength response through combined binder and aggregate configurations. The fitted models showed coefficients of determination of 0.81 for compressive strength, 0.91 for split tensile strength, and 0.97 for flexural strength, supporting their use for interpreting principal trends within the tested mix range. However, the regression equations should not be treated as generalised prediction or optimisation models outside the investigated experimental domain.

From an application perspective, the modified concretes are best suited for non-structural and lightly loaded components where serviceability, durability, resource efficiency, and waste utilisation are key design considerations. Suitable applications include paver blocks, kerbs, median strips, utility channels, precast service components, and pavement subbase or bedding applications. Among the investigated systems, mixes containing SF showed the most favourable balance between strength retention and durability improvement, while ternary binder systems provided additional sustainability benefit through wider utilisation of industrial byproducts.

The findings should be interpreted within the scope of the experimental programme. The study was conducted under controlled laboratory conditions; therefore, long-term field exposure involving combined chloride ingress, carbonation, wetting-drying cycles, temperature variation, and service loading remains an important direction for future research. The FE-SEM and EDS observations provided qualitative support based on selected representative mixtures, while the regression models were developed from a limited but systematically structured experimental matrix. Future research may therefore focus on surface treatment of rubber particles to improve rubber-paste bonding, long-term field durability assessment, quantitative pore-structure analysis, life-cycle and cost evaluation, and larger datasets suitable for advanced statistical or machine-learning-based optimisation.

The research demonstrates that concrete incorporating waste rubber and SCMs can achieve a practical balance between sustainability, durability, and acceptable mechanical performance when mixture proportions are carefully controlled. The main contribution of this work lies in integrating mechanical testing, durability assessment, microstructural interpretation, and statistical analysis within a single experimental framework, thereby providing a clear basis for evaluating multi-component sustainable concrete systems within practical performance limits.
